projects.objective:
The "ERASMUS + ARTISANAT PAYS DE LA LOIRE" project is supported by the Chamber of Trades and Craftsmanship of Pays de la Loire (CMA PDL).

It concerns four sending organizations that are:
-	the CMA PDL
-	the CFA of the Hairdressing and Aesthetics of Loire-Atlantique
-	the CFA of the Hairdressing of the Sarthe
-	the CFA Martello of the Trades of electricity.
CMA PDL, through its Regional University of Trades and Craftsmanship (URMA), manages 5 Apprentice Training Centers (CFA) on 6 sites: Ste-Luce / Loire, St. Nazaire, Laval, Angers, Le Mans and La Roche-sur-Yon.

The project mainly consists in organizing mobility for apprentices in craft trades and young graduates leaving CFA:
- 190 apprentices will go on short group mobility for 12-day stays,
- 100 young graduates will go on long and single mobility Erasmus Pro on stays of 90 to 180 days (post-apprenticeship, with the status of trainee of vocational training).

During the mobility period, the young people will do an internship at a host company in Europe. Short stays of 12 days will be supervised by attendants, CFA staff.

projects.title_en: PRO-CHALLENGE Reunion Island France
projects.objective:
The Reunion Island Academy reaffirms their willingness to get involved in a process of openness and exchanges with Europe within the framework of a new consortium. Their primary aim is to improve the employability and professional integration of young people from Reunion Island who have completed a vocational training.

The local context is characterized by a very young population, a high unemployment rate and a poorly diversified economic fabric. In addition, vocational courses suffer from a lack of visibility among students, families and potential employers. Our challenge is therefore to respond to the need to prepare young people for mobility towards more favourable economic spaces, but also to renew teaching skills and to enhance vocational education and diplomas. 

This new grouped project is the result of team work between 11 high schools coordinated by the rectorate (DAREIC). Thus they wish to initiate a more global reflection on the pooling of skills and resources as well as the harmonisation of the academic offer in order to make it more attractive to the economic world at local and international level.

projects.title_en: My future is in Europe
projects.objective:
Our long years of experience with Erasmus+ projects has enabled us to reinforce our expertise and interest in this mobility, a source of personal and professional enrichment. The earlier the ability to be mobile is developed by a student, the more fruitful it will be. Learners confront their own culture with that of the host countries, thus showing an open mind to adapt to the local culture that may be different without being radically opposed. It is also a unique opportunity to meet new people and learn how to forge links with them, building a network that makes employment easier.

Our school plays a crucial role in providing that taste for mobility, to also fight against inequalities and to encourage citizenship. This allows our students to be more European than before their mobility, because their future is clearly in Europe. 

Our expertise allows us to transfer and adapt our skills to the needs of other colleagues. We try on a daily basis to improve the quality of our educational offer for students with difficulties, who are demotivated and sometimes drop out of school. The vocational school ‘Lycée les Ferrages’ situated in Saint-Chamas, (7,500 inhabitants) a rural area, is close to big towns (Aix-en-Provence, Marseilles, Avignon). The school welcomes students coming from a dozen towns nearby.
For the last few years The ‘Lycée Les Ferrages’ has been welcoming  students with financial and social difficulties (60% unemployed and working class as well as 60% students with scholarships) and has been affected by a poor public transport available. This youth exchange "Time Travellers III: Biking through History" was a youth exchange for youth in which they explored the history of Western Pommerania in Northeast Germany (along the border of Poland). In this exchange participants learned about the history of the region, which is remarkable in its origins as Germania Slavica, region which was until the 13th century mainly populated by Slavic tribes (so called Wends). Here originated the House of Griffins and became part of the feudal association of the German Empire. This region has also a distinct history of viking conquest, two centuries of Danish rule and a rich history of cities in the Hanse Union. With the history of WWII, its division with a part in Poland and another in the GDR this regions offers an enormous cross over of culture that ridicule nationalistic concepts. We invited to this exchange our young friends from Poland, Czechia, Bosnia and Romania together with their German partners, which took a special interest in this example of mutual history.

Egg feast (şahrıl bayf), an event frequently celebrated in Siirt in the past years, has tended to disappear in recent years. Celebrated in the first week of May, people would go out to the countryside, have picnics, boil eggs in vegetable-dyed waters to obtain eggs of different colors, and these eggs were cracked in different activities. Families of engaged or verbal young people would make a basket of colored eggs and give it to the girl's family as a gift, besides, the young people would play local games and our local culture was kept alive through these activities.

<< Objectives >>

According to Wikipedia, a fairy tale, wonder tale, magic tale, or Märchen is a folklore genre that takes the form of a short story. Such stories typically feature entities such as dwarfs, dragons, elves, talking animals, trolls, unicorns, or witches, and usually magic or enchantments. In most cultures, there is no clear line separating myth from folk or fairy tale. The term is mainly related to children's literature. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_tale). But free encyclopedia misses one important and significant fact.
Fairytales aren’t known for their focus on human rights! They contain lessons: don’t judge someone on their looks; be kind to others. They’re chock-full of warnings: don’t stray from the path; watch out for witches, wolves, and spindles. 
However, as a guide to ethics (the broad principles that govern a fair society) or rights (in terms of individual freedoms to be or to do) they are somewhat lacking. So let’s investigate some of the basic human rights abused in everyday fairy tales:
•	Forced marriage
The (unnamed) girl in Rumpelstiltskin is given in marriage to the man who threatens to cut off her head if she doesn’t spin straw into gold.

projects.objective:
Rapid advancements in geographic information technologies and the availability of satellite data allow for sophisticated capture and analysis of information, providing flexible tools that support decision making for agricultural and natural management, as well as climate change adaptation and mitigation. Remote sensing applications can allow the timely inventory of crop areas and their vegetation status levels, which are essential requirements for allowing early monitoring both at the large and at the parcel scale. Object- oriented classification and its segmentation algorithms, more specifically, represent novel approaches to information extraction from multispectral images that, compared to the traditional pixel-based approaches, allow for the identification of patterns (objects) corresponding to surface features and can then be analysed as such. In agriculture, just to mention a few, it allows the extraction of information related to land cover, crop phenology, other vegetation status indices, water detection.
Aiming at target professionals in the land management sector, with our project we want to fill a current knowledge gap existing in relationship with training methodologie

projects.title_en: Arts, Culture and Identity

<< Objectives >>

Identitätssuche ist eine grundlegende Entwicklungsaufgabe in der Zeit der Jugend. Menschen, die in der Jugendarbeit tätig sind, müssen sich dieses Umstands und den damit verbundenen Verhaltensweisen und Erscheinungsformen jugendlichen Ausdrucks bewusst sein. Künstlerische Ausdrucksformen sind in der Lage, diesen Prozess zu unterstützen und geben den Erwachsenen Methoden an die Hand, mit den Jugendlichen an dieser Suche nach Identität zu arbeiten und non-formale Lern- und Bildungsprozesse zu unterstützen. In diesem Trainingskurs wurden den Teilnehmenden Methoden vermittelt, die sich am Konzept der ästhetischen Forschung orientierten. 

Inhaltlich ging es um die Vermittlung einer gestalttheoretischen Grundlage von Identität nach H. Petzold. Dieses Modell begreift Identität als ein Ich-Gefühl, das auf den Säulen Leiblichkeit, soziale Beziehungen, Arbeit und Leistung, Werte und materielle Sicherheit. Diese fünf Säulen wurden mit künstlerischen Methoden erarbeitet. Dabei wurde Wert darauf gelegt, dass der Materialaufwand möglichst gering bleibt. Die Idee dahinter war, den Teilnehmenden einen möglichst niederschwelligen Zugang zum Thema anzubieten.

Die Ziele unseres Projekts "Building Bridges" waren vielfältig und tief in unserem Verständnis der internationalen Jugendarbeit verankert. Unser Hauptziel bestand darin, einen Beitrag zur Erfüllung des inklusiven Bildungsauftrags der internationalen Jugendarbeit zu leisten. How is exclusion/inclusion created? Are people aware of their behaviour which creates exclusion? And how to boost the behaviour which supports inclusion? 
These are the main questions we are tackling during the 2 phase Youth Exchange project called Werewolves vs Aware Wolves. 

In 2 completely different, but complementary youth exchanges we explored the topic of SOCIAL INCLUSION – the way how we make “others” part of our society and turning them (in our eyes) to “us”: to Europeans, and more importantly “to Humans”.
Our VISION was COMPASSION leading to acceptance of everybody, 
and our GOAL was “To make people step behind their fears and approach everybody with compassion and love.” 

The project allowed participants
1) to research their local realities, shared fears and judgments, 
2) to bring awareness of how one’s behaviour and attitude influence other individuals and whole communities, and
3) a deepening into how we as individuals can become more compassionate and empathic through the practice of mindfulness and meditation.

The project will allow young residents to gain a new, youth perspective on their cities. Not only to participate more actively in urban activities, but above all to initiate and create space for young residents. Thanks to non-formal education tools, participants plan to gradually introduce their peers into the urban "tissue", so that they can discover the youth space themselves, which the existence of many young people negates at all. The stereotypical approach to their cities in the 'non-youth' category automatically excludes young people from urban space. On the other hand, decision-makers, NGOs and the media, seeing no young people in this space, stop directing their activities to them. Participants plan to radically break this vicious circle through activities with a very youthful tone, built and promoted for young residents by their peers.

With this project we achieved the following objectives:
1 - We teached youngsters how to reduce waste in all 4 mains areas of their life with practical solutions: food; fashion; hygiene; and electronics. We shared practices on zero waste living. With the project, we wanted to make young people of three countries aware of recycling, upcycling, ecological handling of raw materials and waste material. We taught young people how to reduce the amount of waste, which also indirectly affects weather changes in Europe. At the same time, with the help of over-cycled products, we wanted to provide young people with relaxation areas in and around schools - a Hugge atmosphere. Upcycling is a waste management model where the quality of the material is better than before the product is discarded. It is therefore about the processing of already used, waste materials into new products. With this, we have reduced the amount of waste that takes up valuable space in landfills, and we have also reduced the consumption of natural raw materials that we otherwise need to manufacture new products. By over-cycling, we made a significant contribution to reducing pollution and preserving our environment and the planet.

projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

The question of ethnic minority youth's social and economic interaction with the host communities has received considerable attention over the past few years. Young people with different national and ethnic minority background face the unique issues that demand additional efforts to help them feel safe, welcomed, and use the full extent of labour market opportunities. More than that, they are less likely to participate in different volunteering programs. One of the most common reasons for non-participation among ethnic minority youth is that they do not feel safe, understood, or accepted. They may also feel uncomfortable interacting with other youth that are different from them; they may be less likely to feel understood. That is why we, as an experienced partnership, undertook this project intended to empower young people facing discrimination with skills and knowledge required to advocate their social and economic rights.

Based on our research and survey among youth, we have concluded that while young people are aware of climate change and the issues arising from lack of inclusion, there is a need for more knowledge about practical tools and practices for dealing with these issues on a personal level. The youth expressed a desire to make sustainability a guiding principle of their lives rather than just a one-off occurrence. This highlights the importance of providing systematic education, skills, and habits to support sustainability. The youth exchange delved into the topic of sustainability in-depth and explored its application in daily life, with a focus on real practices to combat climate change, promote inclusion, and contribute to the UN SDGs.
Furthermore, we asked respondents to provide comments on what they would like to learn about sustainability, and we identified two main themes. The first is that youth would like to discover new ways to care for the environment, animals, and engage in gardening as part of their daily routine. The second is that they are interested in concrete examples of sustainable cities and how to live a sustainable lifestyle in urban areas.

Consumption habits are in a position to be effective in all areas and to interfere with the private living spaces of individuals. Policies created for consumption habits in the globalizing world negatively affect the living habits of individuals. The fact that the fashion industry forces individuals to have a perfect beauty towards their body features negatively affects their psychological and physiological characteristics. Thanks to the technologies and regulatory controls called disciplinary society, biopower comes to life in bodies, dominates, and spreads power from inside to outside through individuals, each of whom becomes a policy. The control system is spread throughout the community and manifests itself in the pressure of the neighborhood, from the peer groups at the school, from the workplaces to the courses. As the intensity of the pressure increases, the acceleration in the consumption behavior of individuals increases. In order to get rid of these phenomena, we must strive for the formation of conscious individuals independent of the sanctions of biopower.

We observed that everyone throws away very large amounts of plastic and glass packaging in their homes. We wanted the project to make us aware of the scale of this phenomenon locally and globally and to influence our attitudes and those of our peers. During the project, we developed methods to reuse glass and plastic packaging in creative ways and made fabric shopping bags with our own hands from unused, old materials. We proved to ourselves and others that various objects, even inconspicuous ones, can be given a new, creative life rather than being thoughtlessly thrown in the bin. As we come from small towns, we cannot develop our interests in paid extracurricular activities, so the Erasmus+ project was an ideal alternative for us. Global warming's main cause is the increasing greenhouse effect, primarily due to carbon emissions, known as carbon footprint. Since more than half of greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, reducing carbon dioxide emissions is crucial in combating global warming.

Carbon footprint measures the damage inflicted on the environment in terms of carbon dioxide emissions resulting from human activities. It has two components: primary and secondary footprint. The primary footprint consists of "direct" CO2 emissions from the burning of fossil fuels used for household energy consumption and transportation (cars, planes, etc.). The secondary footprint includes "indirect" CO2 emissions from the production processes of products we use, as well as their subsequent use, waste disposal, and decay processes.

In our project, our aim was to emphasize the importance of the issue to our participants and the people they interact with through activities. During the project, participants were provided with technical information on topics such as Global Warming, Greenhouse Effect, and Carbon Footprint. The number of garments produced annually has doubled since 2014 and estimated 92 million tons of textile waste is created annually from the fashion industry. Every second, the equivalent of one garbage truck of textiles is landfilled or burned globally. In total, up to 85% of textiles go into landfills each year. Washing clothes, meanwhile, releases 500,000 tons of microfibers into the ocean each year — the equivalent of 50 billion plastic bottles. A 2017 report from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) estimated that 35% of all microplastics — very small pieces of plastic that never biodegrade — in the ocean came from the laundering of synthetic textiles like polyester. In the end, the fashion industry is responsible for 10% of humanity's carbon emissions, more than the emission produced from all international flight and maritime shipping combined.

Today, numerous items, including fashion, are obtained swiftly through the phenomenon of “fast fashion”. This mass-production model relies on inexpensive materials and labour to generate new collections quickly. Over the past three decades, clothing has become more affordable, with fashion brands escalating both online and offline production and purchasing. Unfortunately, this has led to a staggering 400% increase in clothing waste in the last 20 years, equivalent to a truckload of clothes entering landfills every second. Projections suggest that by 2030, more than 134 million tonnes of textiles will be discarded annually. Despite the industry's $3 trillion value, it ranks as the second-largest global contaminant, surpassed only by oil, primarily due to environmental neglect in the pursuit of profit.
The manufacturing process exacerbates the problem, as fabrics are dyed using cheap and toxic substances, making the fashion industry the second-largest polluter of clean water, following agriculture. The CoPART project addressed the structural, demographic, and economic challenges faced by Halle, Germany, and Kozani, Greece. Both cities have experienced economic decline due to the transition away from lignite-based industries, leading to reduced employment opportunities and youth migration to larger urban centers. These issues have contributed to demographic decline and weakened community structures. Despite these challenges, both cities are rich in cultural heritage and creative potential, offering opportunities for sustainable development.
Youth unemployment in Europe remains a critical issue, with 614,000 unemployed young people in Greece and 149,000 in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, recorded in 2022. Both regions also face difficulties retaining young talent, as many university graduates leave for better prospects. This "brain drain" exacerbates the demographic challenges and limits the potential for local rejuvenation. Recognizing these issues, CoPART aimed to empower young people aged 18-30 by leveraging culture and creative industries as tools for economic and social transformation.

According to survey data, up to 43% of young people expressed a lack of trust in their local municipal government (M. Polešenský, Iuventa, Conference Are Children Only Our Future?). This trend was confirmed in practice through our youth work at KC PRIESTOR, where we have been engaging with children and young people aged 11 and above (starting from sixth grade) since 2016. The reasons most often cited for this distrust included information consumed via social media—some of which was accurate, while other content amounted to misinformation or even fabricated hoaxes.

In addition, young people reported a lack of meaningful connection with local government, both in online and offline environments. They did not know the individuals elected to represent them, lacked awareness of municipal competencies, and were often unaware of their own rights or the influence they could exert over the city's functioning. projects.title_en: Partir en voyage: pourquoi pas moi ?
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

Our project targets young people living in priority neighborhoods from the city of Nîmes, who often face socio-economic obstacles. It aims to broaden their horizons and boost their self-esteem by offering them a supervised mobility opportunity prepared in collaboration with them. We want them to benefit from a European experience and discover the opportunities offered by the European Union for young people.

The project will be carried out in close collaboration with local associations in Nîmes that already have a relationship of trust with our target group. These associations, which are used to working with young people, will provide them with tailored support before, during and after their mobility, helping them to overcome obstacles and develop their social skills. Youth workers from these associations will accompany the young people during their mobility.

Two mobility routes will be organized, the first on the theme of "gastronomy and feminism" and the second on the theme of "sport and health". Both will aim to develop young people's cross-disciplinary skills, not only through mobility, but also through the preparation and construction of the project.

projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

Projekt miał na celu umożliwienie młodzieży o mniejszych szansach wzięcia udziału w programie mobilnościowym. Naszym celem było nie tylko zapewnienie uczestnikom doświadczeń edukacyjnych, ale także wsparcie ich rozwoju osobistego, poprawy kompetencji językowych, zawodowych oraz społecznych, co miało pozytywnie wpłynąć na ich przyszłość edukacyjną i zawodową. Chcieliśmy dać młodzieży możliwość przezwyciężenia barier geograficznych, społecznych, ekonomicznych i emocjonalnych, które często ograniczają ich szanse na zdobycie międzynarodowego doświadczenia.
Projekt miał na celu stworzenie bezpiecznego i wspierającego środowiska, w którym młodzież mogła rozwijać umiejętności miękkie, takie jak komunikacja, współpraca w grupie, zarządzanie stresem, ale także podnieść swoje kompetencje językowe i zawodowe. Chcieliśmy, aby każdy uczestnik mobilności zyskał nie tylko nowe umiejętności i doświadczenia, ale także pewność siebie oraz motywację do dalszego rozwoju. Projekt miał umożliwić im eksplorowanie nowych środowisk kulturowych i edukacyjnych, budując postawy otwartości, zrozumienia dla innych kultur oraz umiejętność współpracy w międzynarodowych zespołach.

projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

Geschlechterungleichheit wurde als Diskriminierung aufgrund des Geschlechts definiert, was bedeutet, dass Frauen und Männer allein aufgrund von Geschlechterstereotypen unterschiedlich behandelt wurden. Sie hatte Auswirkungen auf verschiedene Aspekte des täglichen Lebens und blieb auch im 21. Jahrhundert ein Problem. We carried out our "TIME TO EMPATHIZE" project in an effort to understand disabled people from the perspective of our own unique experiences. The project aimed to raise awareness among disabled individuals by organizing activities with a group of 5 participants and a group leader from our institution, alongside 4 foreign partners. In total, 30 people participated in the project. The activities took place from December 11th to 20th, 2023, lasting for 10 days.

Even though people from all walks of life encounter disabled individuals, many sadly ignore them or pass by without acknowledging their presence. While some in society do try to communicate, their lack of understanding of an empathetic approach leads them to use pitying language, which makes disabled people feel uncomfortable.
This lack of knowledge about empathy and the prevalence of unhealthy communication creates a negative experience for disabled people, often leading them to feel ostracized and confined to their homes.  In 2020, the EU produced 505 kilograms of municipal waste (including food, wood, paper, textiles, plastics, and rubber) per person. Less than half of this waste, 47.8%, was recycled. The remainder of the waste was either buried or incinerated. The Commission estimated that 600 million tons of such waste could be reused. Transforming waste into resources was seen as a crucial step in achieving a circular economy.

Lithuania (LT) saw an increase in municipal waste from 387 kg per person in 2005 to 483 kg in 2020, with only 45.1% being recycled. Slovakia (SK) experienced a rise from 273 kg to 433 kg per person, with 42.2% being recycled. Hungary (HU) managed to slightly reduce its municipal waste production to 403 kg, with a recycling rate of 32%. Romania (RO) reduced its waste production from 383 kg to 287 kg, but only 13.7% was recycled. Portugal (PT) increased its waste production from 452 kg to 513 kg, surpassing the EU average, with a recycling rate of 26.5%. All the participating countries were below the EU27 average recycling rate of 47.8%.

The project addresses the needs  and common ideas  from 4 groups of youth from Romania, Poland, Croatia and  N. Rep. of Macedonia  in raising awareness regarding to the fast fashion.
Clothes shopping used to be an occasional event-something that happened a few times a year when the seasons changed or when  outgrew what we had. But about 20 years ago, something changed. Clothes became cheaper, trend cycles sped up, and shopping became a hobby. Enter fast fashion and the global chains that now dominate our high streets and online shopping. 
Fast fashion can be defined as cheap, trendy clothing that samples ideas from the catwalk or celebrity culture and turns them into garments in high street stores at breakneck speed to meet consumer demand. The idea is to get the newest styles on the market as fast as possible, so shoppers can snap them up while they are still at the height of their popularity and then, sadly, discard them after a few wears. It plays into the idea that outfit repeating is a fashion faux pas and that if you want to stay relevant, you have to sport the latest looks as they happen. We believe that this project was very useful for all project participants, as young participants, with the help of youth leaders, addressed the issue of fast fashion and discussed the reasons why it happened in the first place and how we ourselves can help to improve the situation.

We want them to stop saying to themselves: "Why should I do something for nature when others don't?" but to replace it with the sentence: "What can I do to be an example to others and to motivate them?" People these days look very much to others and wait for everyone else to start before they can start. We want to create a feeling in our participants that they too are part of the change that we so badly need and to motivate them to "greener" behaviour. We will show them what we are leading to if we do not change, we will provide them with facts, we will educate them, give them practical tasks, workshops and leave them room for discussion. While the first exchange focused on environmental issues, this youth exchange centered on economic and social challenges, still inherently tied to sustainability.

The Sustainable Development Goals tackled were: No Poverty, Zero Hunger, Decent Work and Economic Growth, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, and Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions.

The Eurolab project was created in Gravina in Puglia, a rural and socially peripheral town in Southern Italy, marked by high youth outmigration and a fragmented social fabric, often affected by disillusionment, marginalisation, and low civic participation. In this context, young people who continue their studies tend to move to larger Italian or European cities, while those who remain — often facing early school leaving or social exclusion — express a deep sense of detachment from institutions and a limited involvement in democratic life.

Eurolab was conceived not only as a response to pressing territorial needs, but also as an initiative fully aligned with the priorities of the Erasmus+ programme, particularly those promoting social inclusion, youth participation, and the development of key competences for lifelong learning.

L'Union Européenne produit annuellement 12,6 millions de tonnes de déchets textiles, dont 5,2 millions de tonnes proviennent de vêtements et de chaussures. Cela équivaut à environ 12 kilos de déchets par personne par an, avec seulement 22 % collectés pour le recyclage. Les conséquences environnementales incluent une utilisation excessive d'eau, des substances toxiques dans les tissus, des émissions polluantes, et la libération de microplastiques dans la mer lors du lavage.
La Commission Européenne, dans son "Green Deal", cible la mode, notamment la "fast fashion", en raison de son impact environnemental. L'UE vise à rendre tous les textiles commercialisés durables et recyclables d'ici 2030, avec des fibres recyclées, sans substances nocives, et respectant les droits sociaux et de l'environnement. La France, leader européen, a mis en place la loi AGEC en 2022 pour lutter contre le gaspillage et favoriser l'économie
circulaire. Cette loi impose aux producteurs, importateurs et distributeurs de remettre, réutiliser ou recycler les invendus, avec des sanctions pour les pratiques à usage unique. Ces mesures ont pris effet en janvier 2025.

projects.title_en: On the safe side

The main goal of our project was to educate young people on how to act safely and responsibly during and after natural disasters, as well as in situations caused by human error. The idea for the project was born during a youth group's trip through regions in Poland (Chojnice and Rytel), where we witnessed the long-term effects of a devastating hurricane. Our interest deepened after learning about other natural disasters, such as the Central European Flood of 1997 and the recent earthquake in Marrakesh. These events made us reflect on how unprepared we would be in similar circumstances and how little knowledge we had about emergency response or even basic first aid. We quickly realized that this was not only our problem—young people in general, especially those traveling or living abroad, may find themselves at risk if they don’t know local procedures, especially when facing language barriers.

According to research, the fashion industry accounts for 10% of global carbon emissions, with over 85% of textiles ending up in landfills annually (https://tinyurl.com/3px6myfu.)
Fast fashion is using up natural resources, harming the environment, and creating lots of waste. Brands like Shein, H&M and Zara make cheap clothes very quickly, which makes people, especially young ones, buy more than they actually need. This way of shopping is not good for the planet and is causing serious damage.

The exploitation of workers in developing countries is another serious issue tied to fast fashion. Research shows that many garment workers, especially women and children, are subjected to unsafe working conditions and are paid extremely low wages. This problem highlights the need for more ethical production practices within the fashion industry (https://goodonyou.eco/impact-fast-fashion-garment-workers/)

This results in extreme temperature rises, rising sea levels, extreme weather events, droughts, and floods. Children's rights emphasize that every child has fundamental rights such as health, education, security, and participation, representing a specific aspect of human rights. Problems such as increased natural disasters, food insecurity, and the depletion of water resources directly and indirectly affect children. Issues like rising sea levels, extreme weather events, and ecosystem degradation jeopardize the living spaces and natural resources of future generations.

Although awareness-raising activities were carried out, no stable inclusive Judo structure existed in Luxembourg. We wanted to be a trusted partner who offers clear structure, good preparation and safe learning spaces for both young people and youth workers.

A very important aim was inclusion. We wanted to reach more young people and youth workers with fewer opportunities and give them a real chance to take part. After the principle movements period, it creates purposeful movements in the basic movements period. During human development, the positive development of sensory systems and motor perception enables the person to create purposeful movements. projects.title_en: Wear the Future
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

The project 'Wear the Future' addresses the growing issue of clothing consumption and textile waste in Europe, where fast fashion drives overconsumption. Europeans buy an average of 26 kilos of clothing each year, discarding 11 kilos, with 87% of this waste ending up in landfills or incinerated. Fast fashion, accelerated by social media, has significant environmental and social impacts. In response, the EU introduced a 2022 strategy to promote sustainable textiles and circular economy principles. Additionally, the European Parliament has called for stronger measures on human rights, environmental standards, and mandatory textile collection by 2025.

This project will equip youth workers from six countries with the knowledge and tools to raise awareness about the challenges facing the European fashion industry. Through an intensive training, participants will learn about the environmental effects of fast fashion, the circular economy, and relevant EU policies, such as the 2022 textile strategy. The training will also provide youth workers with educational resources from Fashion Revolution's RecyCOOL Academy to help them apply this knowledge in their local communiti
projects.topics: Green skills; Human rights and rule of law; Environment and climate change

projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

In a context where the economic crisis caused by COVID-19 has deepened a global crisis of values, we see a rise in racist and xenophobic discourses, with the far-right gaining influence. This social and political shift is worrying, as it leads to the polarization and dehumanization of certain groups.

From the perspective of youth work, "Migrate and Resist" seeks to empower this generation to build more inclusive societies. Our goals include framing migration within its historical context, promoting cultural diversity, and understanding migration concepts. We aim to demystify misconceptions, build a positive narrative around migration, and prevent discrimination through inclusive education.
By aligning with the Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, our approach focuses on working with partners to promote the rights of migrants and empower all those involved in building a more equitable society. Our vision is to achieve profound change both in the political sphere, ensuring the well-being of migrants and non-discrimination, and in the social sphere, where education and awareness are key to change.

projects.title_en: Live, Act, and Think Responsibly
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

In recent years, as the global climate crisis and health problems have intensified, the food we consume has gained increasing importance, not only in our country and Europe but worldwide. The modern lifestyle, along with changes in social life and consumer habits (such as the fast and easy access to ready and processed foods, and the increasing participation of both men and women in the workforce), plays a significant role in our eating behaviors. In recent years, there has been a rise in dining out, ordering food at home, and purchasing more food than necessary.
Many of these issues have been further exacerbated by the increase in e-commerce, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw significant growth in online food ordering and grocery shopping. This trend has led to a greater focus on the environmental consequences of our consumption patterns. According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s (FAO) 2021 Food Waste Index Report, 17% of the food produced globally in 2019 was wasted, amounting to approximately 931 million tons. Turkey alone accounted for 8 million tons of household food waste, ranking first in Europe for food waste.

projects.title_en: From Food Waste 2 Food Taste
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

Imagine going to the store, buying three bags of groceries, and then throwing one away the moment you get home. This is essentially what’s happening on a global scale. Around a third of all food produced for human consumption is wasted. But it’s not just the food that’s lost—wasting food also means wasting the resources used to grow, process, and transport it, such as water, energy, and land. When this wasted food ends up in landfills, it decomposes and releases harmful greenhouse gases, contributing to climate change. In fact, if food waste were a country, it would be the third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases, just behind China and the United States. That means food waste contributes more to global emissions than almost any other country on Earth. Simple changes can make a big difference. Leftovers can be saved for the next day, and many food items can be frozen to extend their life. Across the European Union, 88 million tonnes of food are discarded each year, amounting to a financial loss of around 143 billion euros. By reducing food waste, we not only save money but also conserve the resources used to produce it, while lowering our environmental impact.

projects.title_en: Bosques para o Futuro

<< Objectives >>

"Forests for the Future" is a project of vital importance, great motivation, and necessary action. Humanity is investing heavily in technology to collect water, capture carbon emissions, pollinate, and prevent fires... when there is a very simple solution: planting trees and restoring biodiverse forests, especially in peri-urban areas, which serve as the lungs of cities. As of today, the amount of forest we use is infinitely greater than the amount we plant. Additionally, the management of existing plantations is unsustainable in the long term, acidifying and eroding the soil, increasing desertification, and severely impacting ecosystems. Native forests are shrinking, and those that are not monocultures of eucalyptus or pine are abandoned and overrun by invasive species. This is a severe global crisis, yet most young people remain unaware of the magnitude of the problem.  

For this reason, two groups of young people from different regions have come together to take action in regenerating our territories, both near and within cities. We aim to raise awareness among more young people about this issue and its solutions, demonstrating that change is indeed possible.

projects.title_en: Identidad en movimiento
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

The main achievement we seek with “identity on the move” is to move beyond the abstract debate on gender equity to generate a personal, embodied, and lasting transformation in young people. We recognize that while there are critical challenges such as the pay gap or violence, many youth initiatives remain limited to verbal expression and fail to reach the roots of inequality. Our aim, therefore, is to revolutionize this approach by using an innovative methodology that enables participants not only to understand inequity, but to feel it in their own bodies and, from there, find the tools to unlearn it.

To this end, the project’s central objective is to position gender expression as the lens through which equity will be analyzed. We want participants to explore how unwritten norms about how to move, dress, or feel according to gender manifest in their daily lives, solidifying stereotypes. The goal is to use social theatre and body expression as the primary vehicle for this exploration, creating a playful and safe platform where young people can investigate, question, and rehearse new ways of being and relating—away from restrictive roles that perpetuate inequity.

Monitoring of daily consumption – participants observe and record their own behaviours, making the impact of everyday choices visible.
Educational and practical activities – non-formal methods such as debates, workshops, and creative labs help them understand the broader context of sustainability and test accessible alternatives.

<< Objectives >>

Venice, with its unique historical, cultural, and ecological heritage, is facing serious environmental, social, and economic challenges. Rising sea levels, frequent “acqua alta” events, and the fragile lagoon ecosystem put the city at high risk. Extreme floods, like the 1.87 m tide in November 2019, caused major damage to historical landmarks, disrupted local communities, and threatened socio-economic stability.

Environmental pressures are compounded by social and governance issues. Large-scale projects like Mo.S.E. have concentrated resources in a few solutions, often excluding local communities and small-scale interventions. Pollution from diesel-powered vaporetti and industrial activities further endangers the city’s sustainability.

At the same time, Venice faces depopulation, over-tourism, and social-economic imbalances. While initiatives like the Venice World Sustainability Capital Foundation aim to promote sustainability, local, youth-driven actions are often more effective in fostering resilience, inclusion, and environmental awareness.

We will use art (natural sculpture, land art, video, illustration, visual theatre, among others) as a universal language

In contrast, approximately 5.8 million tonnes of textile products are discarded as waste each year in the EU alone. This equates to 11.3 kilograms of waste per person annually. projects.title_en: Revive & Stay! Keeping Youth Local
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

Depopulation is posing serious issues to rural areas in Europe, especially Bellús in Spain. Urban areas are becoming more and more attractive to young people who are looking for greater social, economic, and educational prospects. The population of rural areas declines as a result of this migration pattern, which has an impact on local economy, lowers the provision of services, and weakens community cohesion. Bellús, a town in the Vall de Albaida region, is a prime example of these difficulties due to its declining population and the ensuing economic stagnation. Depopulation has a profound impact not only on the immediate community but also on the broader regional and national levels. It leads to a vicious cycle where the loss of young people diminishes the workforce, reduces innovation, and weakens the social fabric of rural communities. This project aims to break that cycle, empowering youth workers with the skills, knowledge, and resources to encourage young people to stay and thrive in their rural areas. Model aircraft activities worldwide began in 1905 with the establishment of the CIAM (Commission Internationale Aeromodelling) Model Aircraft Committee under the FAI (Federation Aeronautique Internationale) in France. In 1930, the British Royal Navy developed a radio-controlled UAV called the Queen Bee to help pilots practice targeting. In 1939, the United States developed a radio-controlled model aircraft named Radioplane OQ-2.

In Turkey, aviation activities began under the directives of the Great Leader Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, with the establishment of the Turkish Aeronautical Association (Türk Hava Kurumu) on February 16, 1925, the Türkkuşu General Directorate on May 3, 1935, and the Model Aircraft School in the same year. Across our partnership, young people want to cut plastic waste in their daily lives and youth spaces, yet they lack simple, inclusive ways to do it consistently. The scale of the issue is unambiguous. In the European Union, plastic packaging waste per person rose by 26.7 percent between 2011 and 2021, while recycling gains did not keep pace, showing that end-of-pipe fixes alone cannot close the gap. Packaging waste volumes continued to grow through 2022, with plastic recording the highest relative increase among major materials. 

Policy signals are strong but do not automatically translate into everyday practice in youth work. The Single-Use Plastics framework sets separate collection targets for plastic bottles of 77 percent by 2025, rising to 90 percent by 2029, and requires recycled content in beverage bottles (25 percent PET by 2025 and 30 percent for all plastic bottles by 2030). In parallel, the European Union has enacted a restriction on intentionally added microplastics, with key provisions applying from 17 October 2023, covering items such as loose plastic glitter and certain microbeads to reduce releases at the source. projects.title_en: Creativity in Action
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

As professor of psychology Csikszentmihalyi says, creativity does not happen inside people’s heads but in the interaction between a person’s thoughts and a sociocultural context. As his term “flow” defines, when a person is completely absorbed in an activity at hand and the situation, then the person is at full concentration, thus, being the happiest one. projects.title_en: Amplify! – Podcast & Video Tools for Stronger Youth Voices
projects.objective:
<< Objectives >>

The project Amplify! responds to an urgent need in the European youth field: the lack of accessible, structured, and youth-friendly digital communication skills among youth workers and organisations. Today, young people increasingly consume and shape information through social media, podcasts, and short-form videos. If youth organisations cannot master these tools and formats, they risk losing visibility, relevance, and the ability to connect with their target groups.
This gap exists because most youth workers have not received systematic training in digital communication. As partners have observed, “it is not enough to connect a microphone to a phone to create a podcast.” Effective use of digital media requires technical knowledge, narrative design, and communication strategies that youth workers often lack. This leads to frustration in daily practice: organisations struggle to showcase their activities in formats that are youth-friendly, low-barrier and accessible.

projects.objective: The idea that menstruation is dirty, shameful and unmentionable keeps girls and women away from school and out of the workforce. A woman without access to sanitary products may have to stay at home during her periods, while a garment worker risks losing her job for getting off to change her pad before break time, provided there are facilities for her to manage her menstruation at all. Even women working in office environments and girls in schools with conveniently located toilets and flexible schedules go to great lengths to hide periods. Our societies need to be re-educated about menstruation, re-frame its purpose and allow women to be women without any stigma. If open conversation erodes taboos, this project offers one way to get people talking and be re-educated about menstrual health and hygiene. Such conversations and education can't be designed by men for women or by women for women; both men and women need to participate in designing, implementing and monitoring conversations and education around menstrual health and hygiene. projects.title_en: Learn by Design
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.objective:
Loose Part Theory has originally been suggested by Simon Nicholson in 70’s as an architectural approach and later it influenced the game researchers and professionals who design play areas for kids. Nicholson believes that Loose Parts strengthens creativity. In a game, Loose parts can be switched, moved, lined up, redesigned, decomposed into its parts and recombined many times in many variations.
 A requirement for a manual while using the Loose Parts alone or with other materials can not be mentioned. These can be natural or synthetic materials found in the environment of early childhood education. For instance, they may be stones, blocks, beads, lofts, sand, pebbles , fabric, wood, timber, palette, flowers, ropes, thick ropes, tree branches, boxes, baskets, rubber bands, balls, shells, seeds etc. Loose Materials at playgrounds enables children to use them as they wish. Most of the time, kids prefer playing with adaptable and readily available materials rather than expensive or commercial toys . Children who are playing with Loose parts have higher chance to use creativity, imagination while developing skills and competence than the ones playing with the most modern plastic toys.

A diet comprised of fibre-rich food such as leafy green salads, vegetables and whole grains has been consistently associated with a reduced risk for depression. At the same time an unhealthy diet high in processed food and high fat dairy has previously been found to be associated with increased odds for depression. projects.objective: Our world has been struggling with lack of oxygen recently. Cities are faced with many negative factors that pollute the air such as population, transportation and industry. Especially industrial products are in many areas of our lives and we are faced with the negative effects of them in indoor places. Chemicals such as rhodone gas, benzene, ammonia and trichloroethylene coming out of objects such as detergents, building materials, and fabrics used indoors threaten our health. projects.title_en: Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Student Ambassador Programme
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.objective:
Across Europe there are issues with discrimination in schools based on people’s background and identities, this stems from a lack of awareness and understanding of equality, diversity, and inclusion (ED&I) issues such as migration, race, refugees, disabilities, ethnicity, religion, LGBT+, sexuality, gender and poverty. This project brings together at least 150 students aged 15-19 from 6 schools to become ED&I ambassadors, challenge discrimination and increase awareness of ED&I. Our key aims are to promote ED&I; tackle discrimination; and to encourage social action and social/community responsibility amongst students and staff. Additionally, we are committed to prioritising students from disadvantaged backgrounds including refugees, migrants, religious-minorities, ethnic minorities, students with disabilities, students from low-socioeconomic backgrounds and students likely to drop out of school or less likely to continue into higher education. 

In the first year of the project schools will appoint student ED&I ambassadors who will learn about a different ED&I theme each month and devise strategies to raise awareness of these themes in their schools and communities.

<< Background >>

The TCLF industries suffer from an attractiveness deficit due to an outdated image and ongoing misconceptions which does not appropriately reflect the modernity and competitiveness of these industries and the large variety of career opportunities that they offer today. << Background >>

The background of the ALBATTS project is the emerging battery- and electromobility value chain in Europe, which is a crucial element in EU climate- and transport policy. Europe had previously very little industrial activity in this value chain, and battery cell production was especially missing. For this, new skills and occupations are needed in the European workforce. While the time spent in nursery, then at school and in recreational centers is steadily increasing for children, their "outdoor" time decreases. The courtyard is often the only place where children can freely play outside. However, this is a pedagogically disinvested place, poor in games, where "chaos" reigns and which is, in fact, a very "accident-prone" and stressful place for educational teams. Meanwhile, our society produces more and more objects and as a result, we can observe the increase of waste of all kinds: unsold factory stock, default objects, packaging, objects that are old-fashioned ... All these fields of cooperation are very important for improvement of quality and attractiveness of initial VET in the different countries. However, along with its use also comes a call for responsible action. New environments require new guidelines and expectations. This is something that our students must learn, as it can not be assumed that they will put the new practices into their online interactions naturally. Digital literacy encompasses the skills that our students must learn in order to engage independently, responsibly, critically, and creatively in this new digital landscape, both as consumers as well as producers. This Project followed the footprints of the Roman Empire in the European Union in order to emphasize that although the countries are separated from each other by borders in our era, they stick to each other with a stronger bond: history. We chose partners from countries which were once a part of the Roman Empire (RE). For 3 years, students and teachers from 9 partner countries discovered and overcame the borders of the largest and most powerful empire of the ancient world and both reconstructed and experienced the RE’s vast cultural heritage. By cooperating on an international level and visiting each other, the participants had the opportunity to discover the traces and influences of the RE on our culture, language, literature, social life, religion and architecture. So, we made some excavations to RE, the most important common point among partner countries, in order to make our students understand the importance of heritages in their own countries and then to learn to appreciate the others' values and finally understand that they share a similar background with others and this collective and shared history make them a unite in spite of cultural or social differences.

Our thesis was: The best way to counteract such anxieties and promote tolerance is to seek further knowledge about your own culture by sharing it with others. 

This is an issue not least for a minority culture like the small Sorbian community in Germany, but also for the Norwegians, who are a small people in Europe and at the same time a majority culture in their own country with a Sami indigenous population.  
By exploring our own culture and comparing it with another, both parties benefited: Tolerance springs from self-awareness and mutual understanding. Sharing means increased knowledge, understanding, respect and, ultimately, a wish to preserve what is valuable. These needs were taken into account in our project by practically approaching the six sub-topics examining the concrete execution of ideas for integration.

The environment is mainly rural and the activities of the inhabitants are mostly concentrated in the primary sector, agriculture in particular. Many of our students live on farms located in marginal areas and poorly connected by roads, which is why they are very often forced to spend their free time alone, unlike students who live in more central areas. Previously loved items deserve a second chance to inspire us again; people with mental health problems deserve a second chance to take control of their life. In today's throw-away society it seems that nothing is valuable, that we can change our clothes or even the people around us in the blink of an eye. We want people to return to valuing what is all around them; show them that creativity, lifelong learning and empathy are powerful tools than can change the world!

Chic&Craft is an on-line training course specially designed for people with mental health issues which aims to re-use and recycle second-hand clothes and waste materials, creating a unique European fashion brand where hand-craft designs and original creations play a major role. projects.title_en: Collect. Recycle. Manufacture.
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.objective:
One of the biggest global problems in the world is the increasing felling of forest areas, where the wood is used for paper production. Another important issue is the growing paper consumption and excessive consumerism. During the project all learners analyzed situations in their countries and shared their experiences with other participants from partner countries. Project participants learned to produce handmade paper out of collected waste-paper and taught other members of community to do the same. 
We encouraged the learners to look back to the past. Using our ancestors’ wisdom, we learned to produce ecological dyes extracted from herbs and ground pigments. The idea for DIVERSITY arose from pressing needs identified in the AE environment a few years into the management of special programmes aimed at refugees. Migration is not a new topic, but especially since 2015, the increased influx of migrants and refugees put it on a new level. The sudden increase of immigrants from different educational, economic and cultural contexts created mechanisms of rapid response to emergency situations and contingencies. Those emergencies were and still are being answered with a plethora of language and cultural awareness courses to promote integration. Professional Training and certified courses for low-qualified workers in several industrial sectors are nowadays focussed in technical skills to cope with these sectors' demands, most of them with a strong growth as wind energy. Nevertheless, the psychological requirements of some of the most in-demand positions are very important in the worker´s performance (e.g., emotional pressure, anxiety, monotony, isolation, intense working periods, etc.). In addition, employees are expected to develop some psychosocial competencies to overcome these psychological requirements that are not covered by certified training courses (e.g., decision-making or time management). As a result, there is a rapid burnout of workers and a high attrition rate in this type of positions. And even worse, the lack of well-developed psychosocial competences sometimes ends in risky situations and occupational accidents.

<< Background >>

The spread of the coronavirus pandemic has caused disruption in many plants, broken supply chains and prevented production at many industrial factories. In a time of global crisis, it forces most companies to review their current working methods and consider implementing new tools and technologies...... Such as 3D printing (Additive Manufacturing (AM)).

This project was motivated by the current pandemic and Eurostat data (2018) that indicated that the use by enterprises of 3D printing in EU countries ranges wildly from very low use in Cyprus to very high use in Finland. The EU-28 average was only 27%. There is therefore a need to undertake an integrated European approach to this issue to ensure ‘Training Consistency '. As the 3D printing industry booms, what does it mean for job seekers? 

What good are these jobs if no one has the qualifications to fill them? To help fill the skills gap 3D printing programs at all grade levels need to develop and widely offered. This will open jobs for educators who can teach the technical and business aspects of 3D printing. The possibilities and opportunities that 3D printing is creating in education is endless.

projects.title_en: Heliculture Serious Game for the promotion of sustainable snail cultivation businesses focusing on exports
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

Although little-practiced and quite obscure relative to other forms of agriculture, snail farming (also known as heliculture) is a form of farming that in theory bears a lot of promise as a modern business model. It requires relatively little space, start-up resources, or agricultural expertise, and so can be undertaken flexible on a comparatively small scale to start before being scaled up to meet commercial requirements as desired.
The broad issues identified as barriers to snail farming at the inception of this projects were therefore twofold: first, that awareness of snail farming as a potential business activity in Europe is generally very low. Secondly, in practice, many incipient heliculture businesses fail because of a lack of relevant skills or expertise. If these needs were met, it is therefore much more likely that heliculture could become a viable, simple, and flexible business opportunity for many, particularly in rural areas. 
The central driving force behind this project therefore was to promote heliculture as a potential hobby or even business and in particular the skills necessary for this through the use of a serious game.

projects.objective:
The agro-food industry plays an important role in the European Union (EU) economy and is an important sector involved in the achievement of the goals set out by the “Europe 2020” growth strategy. This sector generates about 6% of the EU Gross Domestic Product and employs over 48 million people. Due to new challenges, its economic growth and competitiveness have been under performing compared to the overall EU economy in recent years. One of these challenges is to improve the availability of a skilled workforce. With this project, we addressed three critical issues: (1) too few individuals develop sector-specific qualifications at university level; (2) a gap exists between the skills that are actually required by employers and the curriculum offered by universities; (3) too little communication occurs among relevant stakeholders (e.g., universities, industry and public authorities).

To tackle these issues, we formed a strategic partnership composed of European universities (higher education institutions (HEs)) and industry partners that actively pursue communication among relevant stakeholders. The ABLE Project (2015-2018) focused on the challenge of using learning analytics to support student transition into, during and beyond the first year of university. There is a significant body of research taking place in universities across the sector, but that relatively few had fully embedded that learning into institutional support systems. 

It is important to note that the national contexts profoundly influenced the way that learning analytics was used to support first year students. In the UK, the emphasis was upon supporting first year student retention, in Belgium and the Netherlands, the focus was on study efficiency: ensuring that students were on the right programme. However, in practice the tools were used in similar ways, either by staff members (study advisers or personal tutors) using the learning analytics dashboards with first year students or by students using them independently.

Combining two technologies - recirculating aquaculture systems and hydroponics - in a closed-loop system, aquaponics is a sustainable food production technology which requires a low level of resource input, since the plants receive their nutrients from the fish water. As a soilless cultivation method, aquaponic systems can be used for growing food in cities, and thus could help to reduce carbon emissions and improve food security and the resilience of urban food systems by shortening supply chains. However, in order for aquaponics to develop its potential in Europe, it needs an appropriately trained workforce. The Aqu@teach project aimed to address that need, by developing the first ever aquaponics curriculum specifically for higher education students. In recent years, cultural and creative industries (CCI) have represented an increasingly important employment basin in the EU labour market. They employ around 8.3 million people, equal to 3.8% of the entire EU force, generating an added value of around €558 bn, equal to 4.4% of EU GDP (Mapping the creative value chains. projects.title_en: Decoding the Disciplines in European Institutions of Higher Education: Intercultural and Interdisciplinary Approach to Teaching and Learning
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.objective:
In the course of the Project, it has been established that the Decoding the Disciplines methodology can be used as a practical pedagogical strategy for helping students with difficult material or a basis for research in the scholarship of teaching and learning (or both).
For instance, in the study of immigration history students usually bring an assumption that immigration is a one-directional process similar to an invasion. This assumption can be deconstructed with an example of migration patterns of Monarch butterflies. As soon as students learn that in nature migration is often cyclical, not linear, they become less resistant to learning the history of immigration from a different viewpoint, or that of immigrants.  Similarly, students’ critical reading, which is essential to any academic study, can be improved by helping them understand the difference between description and synthesis of information, or helping them understand how a reasoned argument is structured.  Such approaches can model ways of thinking about a topic or skill that brings new insight and understanding.

The project “Fablab Schools EU: Towards Digital Smart, Entrepreneurial and Innovative Pupils” addresses a need to develop common methodological principles for educational digital fabrication visible across Europe. In many European countries, we see digital manufacturing environments and workshops (FabLab ) shoot up, but there is a need to clarify the pedagogical principles behind educational digital fabrication.

Moreover, this strengthens their entrepreneurial spirit -- two main focus of the EU's Education 2020 strategy, and the Erasmus+ program's goals. When talking about professional networks in our project, we mean open, continuously cooperating groups of teachers within one school and across various schools sharing their experience and materials and cooperating in terms of innovations and development of teaching and learning. Many researchers as well as policymakers underline the importance of internal and external support of networks. projects.title_en: Regional Learning Communities and Facilitators
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

While intercollegial exchange is often institutionalised in other educational settings, a strong lone wolf mentality is prominent in schools. The exchange within or across schools is not a structured form of mutual support, but a selective exchange dependent on mutual sympathy. The potential of guided and structured cooperation is thus not used, which also makes many teachers feel left alone. As a result, a lot of work is done more than once, which would not be necessary if there was better networking and mutual support, so that more time would be available for the pedagogical work with the pupils.

With the project "Regional Learning Communities and Facilitators" our aim was to indirectly support the work of teachers and to make it easier for them to plan, implement and follow up their lessons by focusing on the principles of cooperation and exchange. Through active networking, but also by pointing out opportunities for connection, teachers should no longer have the feeling that they are alone in the field, but rather embedded in a professional system that also gives them more self-confidence and a sense of self-efficacy.

<< Background >>

In 2018, the European Commission (EC) published the "Coordinated Plan on the development and use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Made in Europe", which aimed to maximize the impact and spread the benefits of AI across Europe. In this plan, education played a key role, and two main needs were defined: to prepare more young citizens for studying AI in higher education, and to prepare all of them for living in a world increasingly impacted by AI. These were the needs faced in this project.  

To advance on achieving them, it was proposed the development of a formal AI curriculum for high school students (15 to 18 years old) and teachers. This target educational level was chosen, first, to focus the project scope, being able to carry out a reliable work in a 3-year period. And second, to provide a short-term solution to the target needs. Next high school generations will be the first that will take advantage of having a formal AI background for their future.

The project FROM SEED TO SPOON (S2S) arises from the need to make youngsters more aware on how complex the food system is and to help them to respect and take care of the nature. Taking care of it means gaining back in clean air and water, fertile soils, as well as nutritious, healthy food. Also, since young people are often at high risk of developing disordered eating patterns, another need addressed by S2S is improving mindful and healthy eating habits, encouraging them towards a more healthy diet.

projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices

<< Background >>

In the days of the Athenian polis, public speaking, debate and philosophy were the cornerstones of democratic life. Philosophy had the form of a dialogue between people with contrasting views, and philosophers taught the art of persuasion to citizens attending the ekklēsia—the principal assembly of the democracy of ancient Athens. In contemporary secondary schools however, debate clubs and philosophy classrooms have become separate worlds that, regrettably, seldom interfere. This state of affairs leads to a waste of knowledge and skills, and lowers the potential impact that debating skills and philosophical thinking could have on strengthening democracy.

<< Objectives >>

With our new philosophical debate methodology, we hope to teach students how to apply philosophical concepts to question the status quo, and to discuss social issues in a respectful way with their peers. As such, we hope that the outputs of the ADAPT project will contribute to the development of high school students into engaged, critical and active citizens, and that teachers will find in it an effective tool to facilitate this process.

Online, children can be exposed to harmful content and behaviour such as cyberbullying, sexual harassment, pornography, violence, or self-harm. Thus, efficient responses are needed to prevent negative consequences for their cognitive, social and emotional development.

Surveys reveal that 37% of teachers have already witnessed an online safety incident in their classrooms (sharing personal information or cyberbullying, for example).
Evidence says that in most cases teachers miss the cyber awareness competences and the resources to do it, limiting their power and their will to act. This is what the Global Teachers Survey (2017) also highlights, as 82% of teachers said they didn't feel they had the necessary resources to teach online safety to their students.

As a result of preliminary research, we identified a number of Erasmus projects related to online safety, but usually for older age brackets (teens/youngsters) and most focusing only in specific issues, like cyberbullying. Thus, there are lack of initiatives to help teachers at primary school level.

projects.title_en: Women's Legacy: Our Cultural Heritage for Equity

projects.objective:
<< Background >>

The cultural and social implications of the systematic absence of female references and their productions in all areas of education represent one of the most active mechanisms of discrimination for women and an enormous loss of cultural heritage. A study carried out in 2014 showed that only 7.6% of female references appear in manuals. This represents, on the one hand, a marked cultural loss because ignorance of these productions impoverishes European cultural heritage. On the other hand, this absence constitutes a delegitimization of women and one of the essential aspects of structural inequalities. Farming is the principal economic activity in most rural areas of the EU. About half of the population of the EU lives in rural areas. Without farming there would be little to keep many communities alive and hold them together. If farming were to disappear, in many areas there would be a problem of land abandonment. Therefore, EU’s Common Agricultural Policy supports farmers in many aspects. 

Many farmers are over the age of 55 and will retire from active farming at some point in the future or women who are less educated and do not have entrepreneurship competences. Especially women represent a substantial share of the total agricultural labour force and their contributions are mostly invisible. They are not seen “productive” since they are generally expected to work without payment. This invisibility at the intersection of markets, state and society has suppressed the whole potential of woman farmers worldwide. Helping woman farmers get started is a policy ‘must’ if Europe’s rural areas are successfully to meet the many challenges that face them.

projects.objective:
The European textile industry has always been keen to preserve representative examples of textile production of the past, either for creative or for educational purposes. Numerous collections of antique and exotic textiles, today preserved in museums, have come from the private collections of textile entrepreneurs or industrial institutes and schools. Many firms have also acquired whole archives or textile samples from other sources.

Over the last few decades, the economic crisis which has affected the European textile sector has resulted in the loss of many textile archives. Indeed the failure of businesses and the consequent closure of their warehouses has caused the loss of hundreds of textile samples and designs. In order to avoid breaking the line of continuity which joins past and future textile production - a fundamental feature of European excellence in the fashion sector - it is necessary for museums, cultural institutions and textile companies to protect our textile heritage.

The SKIVRE partnership developed a multi-modular training scheme for manufacturing and marketing high-quality handcrafted products of European monasteries. Monastic heritage represents an important part of European heritage, shared by all EU countries mainly in their rural areas. Monasteries served not only the transmission of the Christian faith but were economic hotspots for the exchange of goods and services. The core concept of this project is to establish support service, to train carers and raise awareness towards elder maltreatment. It is a growing concern, and estimates suggest that at least 4 million people experience elder maltreatment in any one year in the EU Region. The full scale of the problem is not properly understood, but it has far-reaching consequences for the mental and physical well-being of tens of millions of older people and, if left unchecked, may result in their premature death. projects.objective:
<< Background >>

BACKGROUND & CONTEXT 
Feedback loop mechanisms are widely considered as necessary for monitoring and improving the efficiency of VET provision. Graduate tracking plays a key role in this context, as a principal mechanism for generating data on graduates’ employment and further training, skills-matching between training provision and job market requirements, as well as data on the actual efficiency and results of VET provision. However, recent mappings of VET tracking measures across the EU reveal a less than uniform and consistent terrain. 

NEEDS ADDRESSED
InTheLoop4VET intervenes in the field of VET to address providers’ needs for graduate tracking processes leading to provision adaptation. The project rationale encompasses a ‘local’ perspective of empowering providers by addressing their need for meaningful contributions to data generation and data-driven decision-making. Simultaneously, InTheLoop4VET contributes in addressing the need for the development of international standards in graduate tracking. Therefore, InTheLoop4VET adopts a rationale that recognizes the need for local measures, yet integrated into a transnational VET QA framework.

projects.title_en: Reskilling coal industry workers for the renewables energy sector
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.action_type: Strategic Partnerships for vocational education and training
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

BACKGROUND & CONTEXT 
The decarbonisation of the EU27 caused job losses in coal mines and plants, with 81% of the total EU coal workforce affected in Greece, Germany, Austria, Romania, Bulgaria, and Poland. However, the shift towards renewable energy sources (RES) created new job opportunities in the sector, which coal workers could potentially fill due to their similar skill sets. The project aimed to provide reskilling opportunities for coal workers to transition to the RES sector, utilizing their skills such as their durability in hazardous environments and experience with manual and sophisticated technologies. 

NEEDS ADDRESSED
This project addressed the need for job opportunities in the renewable energy sector in Europe, with 304,000 new jobs per year expected until 2030. The wind and solar PV industries were expected to have the highest job growth. Coal-intensive countries had untapped potential for RES jobs, particularly in Germany, Poland, and Greece. Coal-intensive regions in Romania, Bulgaria, and Greece also had untapped potential for RES growth. The project aimed to facilitate the transition of coal workers to the RES sector to address these needs.

Street culture is a rapidly evolving area of economic activity and includes urban arts and creative industries, fashion, food and tourism, all of which offer opportunities for innovative, entrepreneurial start-ups. However, given its informal roots and sometimes negative connotations, it has not been "on the radar" for focused enterprise development. Street Culture tor Regions (SCR) has sought to change this by guiding and equipping entrepreneurship education providers to make the most of street culture opportunities for skills' development and economic and social inclusion in our cities and regions.
