projects.title_en: Women in the Film Industry
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.action_type: Strategic Partnerships for vocational education and training
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

Within the film industry, gender inequalities relating to biased representation and pay are arguably systemic and pervasive.  The representation of women in film projects can be gauged by a test known as the Bechdel-Wallace test. A film passes the test if it features at least two women talking about something other than a man.

This inequality is replicated behind the camera with around a third of available roles taken by women.  However, even here, roles that are traditionally associated with women, such as admin and costume design, show that women are over-represented while they continue to be under-represented in areas such as sound, image and music.

For any women with an eye to a future within the industry, it is crucial that equality is embedded into their reality.  The project partners identified a number of issues that need to be addressed to inspire and encourage women to break through the celluloid ceiling; an understanding of opportunities and how to access them, examples of jobs and roles across the industry, and relatable role models with real life stories being realistic about the struggles but positive about the possibilities.

projects.title_en: FabEdu: digital fabrication in youth work
projects.key_action: Cooperation for innovation and the exchange of good practices
projects.objective:
FabEdu is a european cooperation project that aims to bring innovation in the field of youth work. The initiative is lead by Digijeunes, in partnership with Vectorealism (Italy), Fablab Pau (France), the municipality of Alba Iulia (Romania), and Combustible Numérique (France).  

OBJECTIVES

Over a period of 18 months the project cosortium produced a set of open educational resources on the topic of digital fabrication. The project’s deliverables are expected to facilitate the implementation of educational digital science workshops across Europe, thus contributing to improving digital literacy among youth, and challenging the digital divide. 

RESULTS

We have produced a number of tutorials and physical objects to enable youth workers across Europe to launch their own hands-on workshops on digital fabrication.
Our educational resources rely exclusively on free and open source hardware/software, and are dvided into 3 modules :
- Introductory activites on digital fabrication
- Hands-on activities on 3D modeling, 3D printing, laser cutting, 3D scanning, and traditional DIY
- Tutorials on how to build and use mini diy cnc machines

The project "Fostering Adolescents’ Knowledge and Empowerment in Outsmarting Fake Facts" (FAKE OFF) aimed at fostering young people's internet literacy, creating awareness of intentional misinformation and enabling them to identify “fake news” to avoid them. 
 
BACKGROUND
“Fake news” and “fake facts” have become not only fashionable keywords but actual threats to democratic values. Especially young people, who spend increasing amounts of time on the internet and with social media, are targeted by fake news for propaganda and/or profit reasons. Therefore, they need empowerment and knowledge to outsmart the flow of intentional misinformation through critical thinking and improved internet literacy (e.g. fact-checking abilities). Although initiatives to foster these competencies have been initiated by educators and corporations, adequate didactic means to foster digital literacy skills have been missing in the sphere of youth work until now.

Based on a preliminary needs analysis at three levels, including our organisational experience in the field of youth inclusion and training, a review of relevant national content and EU youth policy, we found that training for youth leaders is usually project-based and takes the form of intensive (1-2 days) training sessions. While this is a valid approach, it raises questions about the sustainability of learning outcomes, especially those related to motivation. The most popular training topics are soft skills; gaining knowledge about how institutions work; event management.
Training for youth workers who train youth leaders does not follow any standardised methodology or framework of learning outcomes, but is usually up to the individual practitioners to decide how to go about it. At the same time, there is a wide range of reasons for the lack of encouragement and motivation of future youth leaders. << Background >>

According to Eurostat (2017), 28% of young people aged 16- 29 years were at risk of social exclusion in the EU. projects.key_action: Partnerships for cooperation and exchanges of practices
projects.action_type: Alliances for Sectoral Cooperation on Skills (implementing the ‘Blueprint’)
projects.objective:
Background
Hydrogen is a key pillar of the EU’s strategy to achieve its 2050 decarbonisation goals, with an estimated 24% of hydrogen contributing to the total energy demand by 2050, 560Mt CO2 abatement per year, 820 bn euro annual revenue generation, and a 15% reduction in local emissions. The rapid development of the European Hydrogen Value Chain over the coming years is expected to generate approximately 1 million highly skilled jobs by 2030, and up to 5.4 million by 2050.  This growth presents a significant economic and environmental opportunity for Europe, but it also creates considerable labour market challenges.  

Objectives
The primary objective of this project is to design and implement a highly innovative, effective, and sustainable Hydrogen Skills Strategy for Europe that will ensure the skills needs of the rapidly expanding and evolving Hydrogen Value Chain can be met in the short, medium, and long term. This blueprint will address the skills need of workers in Declining Sectors and Transition Regions to provide them with upskilling and reskilling opportunities that will enable them to access new employment opportunities within the Hydrogen sector.

EU’s microelectronics ecosystem is undermined by a shortage of professionals, skills mismatches and distance between the worlds of education and work. Aware of those challenges, the EU Commission launched a series of initiatives, above all the launch of a Microelectronics Pact for Skills (2020) and the publication of the “EU Chips Act” (adoption foreseen) to revamp Europe’s microelectronics ecosystem. Yet, the Pact for Skills has yet to deliver on its expectations and innovative approaches towards education and training in microelectronics are required.

By developing a structured AI-driven training framework, the project enables designers, architects, and creative professionals to integrate AI-powered creativity, digital fabrication, and sustainable design into their work.

Through extensive pilot testing, the project refines AI-driven education strategies, integrating certification pathways and accreditation mechanisms to support long-term adoption.

Despite Albania’s rich history of craftsmanship in woodworking, filigree jewelry, stone carving, and textiles, the sector faces declining youth engagement, outdated training, limited digital skills, and weak international recognition. projects.key_action: Partnerships for cooperation and exchanges of practices
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

Contemporary Europe faces numerous challenges, including the rise of populism, which bolsters illiberal democracies. Xenophobia, intolerance, and social fragmentation among culturally diverse populations evoke, for many, unsettling parallels to the pre-World War II era. The refugee crisis of 2015 further deepened ideological divisions within the European project, widening the rift between Western and Eastern member states. Meanwhile, racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, antigypsyism, and other forms of group-focused enmity (GFE) have significantly increased.
Europe's hallmark diversity—reflected in its social, ethnic, and religious heterogeneity—requires urgent efforts to navigate cultural divides and foster shared values. For Europe’s future cohesion, bridging ideological gaps and promoting inclusivity are essential. An integrative approach is needed to reconcile conflicting worldviews and reduce estrangement between ethnocultural minorities and majorities.
This project addresses the urgent need for equality, non-discrimination, and measures to combat xenophobia and intolerance as cornerstones of a resilient European society.

<< Objectives >>

Universities often lack structured approaches to support the development of non-cognitive competencies such as grit, perseverance, self-efficacy, and a sense of social responsibility, especially among young researchers navigating complex academic and social challenges. << Background >>

The textile industry is water intensive, representing 4% of global freshwater withdrawal. Improving environmental performance in the textiles supply chain is critical for the long‐term viability of the sector as well as the sustainability of ecosystems and communities. The water footprint (WF) is a measure of the appropriation of freshwater for production both in terms of the water consumption or pollution. WF assessment is a structured process to quantify the WF, assess its sustainability and use this information to identify strategic actions to reduce the WF and improve sustainability. Therefore, there is an inevitable need to spread knowledge and inform producers about freshwater use and the impact of their activities. WF assessment includes a comprehensive approach to the accounting of water consumption and pollution and strategic response formulation to address the world’s pressing water challenges. Of this total, households contributed around 31 million tonnes of FW (53% of the total), while restaurants and food services accounted for approximately 5 million tonnes. The EU and its Member States are committed to meeting Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 12.3, adopted in September 2015, which targets to halve per capita food waste at the retail and consumer level by 2030, and reduce food losses along the food production and supply chains. To achieve this target, all key players from public and private sectors must work together to better identify, measure, understand and find viable solutions.
The ADVANCE project addressed the following needs:
- Identification of benefits, barriers and best practices in FW management for municipalities and HORECA SMEs.
- Improvement of knowledge and skills of municipal and hospitality sectors in FW management.

The project was initiated to address a critical gap in training opportunities for MSEs, particularly businesses with fewer than 50 employees. While medium-sized enterprises typically benefit from formal or informal training programs, smaller firms, especially micro-companies with up to 9 employees, show little to no participation in such initiatives. This lack of training engagement, both internal and external, is further compounded by a reluctance to accept external advice, which hampers their potential for growth.

By developing a targeted project like LEAD, we aimed to bridge this gap and offer a new, innovative solution in the entrepreneurial environment, helping MSEs recognise the benefits of systematic retraining and adopt a forward-looking vision for their companies' development. The rise of fast fashion has led to massive overproduction and waste, while 87% of clothing ends up in landfills. Our goal was to tackle these challenges through education—starting with the design phase, which determines over 80% of a product’s environmental impact. The project empowers VET learners and trainers with digital tools and AI applications to promote sustainability, reduce waste, and rethink fashion practices. It equips future professionals with the skills to design smarter, work more efficiently, and create value in a more circular and responsible fashion system. AI can support decision-making, reduce unsold stock, and improve forecasting—key for a sustainable transition. This initiative responds to the growing need for greener business models, offering a strategic path to upskilling the workforce while reducing fashion’s environmental and social footprint.

<< Background >>

The LOFT project was developed in response to pressing challenges in food systems, exacerbated by the COVID-19, which highlighted vulnerabilities in global supply chains. Consumers increasingly prioritize healthy diets, food safety and security, while small-scale local food producers (LFPs) struggle to meet traceability and sustainability demands. 
LFPs lacked the digital readiness, infrastructure and networks to adapt to rapidly changing consumer habits and supply chain disruptions. They struggled to transition to digital sales, reach broader markets and ensure food traceability. Meanwhile, consumers have increasingly looked for safer, local food sources, but they have not had access to reliable platforms and guidance. The project addressed important gaps in vocational education, digital transformation, consumer awareness and food security through integrated work packages—ranging from a VET methodology to a multifunctional website/platform.
The background of LOFT is based on: Strengthening local food systems; Equipping LFPs with VET and digital tools; Sustainability awareness of the public; Contribution to structuring data on EU local food sectors.

<< Background >>

Das Projekt wurde ins Leben gerufen, um auf die dringenden Bedürfnisse und Herausforderungen zu reagieren, die durch die Covid19-Pandemie und den daraus resultierenden abrupten Wandel in der Jugendbeteiligung und -bildung hervorgebracht wurden. Durch die Krise wurden bewährte Massnahmen der Jugendbeteiligung gestoppt oder unterbrochen und Fachkräfte sowie Ehrenamtliche fanden sich unvorbereitet auf die Anforderungen digitaler Beteiligungsformate. Die Erfahrung zeigte, dass die notwendigen digitalen Kompetenzen oft nur rudimentär vorhanden waren. Unser Ziel war es, diese Lücke zu schliessen, indem wir Lernelemente (Videos, Quizze), Weiterbildungsformate (Webinare) und eine zentrale Plattform (www.e-parti.eu) entwickelten, um die Kompetenzen der Fachkräfte im Bereich der digitalen Jugendbeteiligung und Jugendbildung zu stärken. Wir wollten damit eine Brücke schlagen zwischen realweltlichen und digitalen Beteiligungsformaten und so den Fachkräften helfen, ihre Arbeit unter den neuen Gegebenheiten erfolgreich fortzusetzen. Die Notwendigkeit für solche Angebote bestand zwar schon länger, doch hat die Pandemie die Dringlichkeit und den Bedarf an digitaler Transformation

The “Designing an International Master in Social Enterprise and Social Economy” (DIMSE) partnership will explore the feasibility of offering a unique joint Master programme on the social economy and social enterprise. Social enterprises refers to the variety of initiatives in many different sectors of activity—work integration, social finance, short supply chains, recycling, personal services, collaborative economy, culture, and many others—whereby citizens, private sector actors, and public officials are carrying out new opportunities to promote societal goals. These initiatives open up new activities that create jobs; inspire trust among citizens and public authorities through a value-based economy and contribute to the institutional plurality of our economic systems, opening the door to citizen involvement, participation, and empowerment. The social economy refers to the wider sphere where these social enterprises and other traditional legal forms (cooperatives, associations, mutual, foundations) emerge and thrive.

A critical element for industries in this context is how they design and optimise their manufacturing engineering, operations and maintenance management. How to make the best use of resources, including energy, to ensure sustainability in line with the European Green Deal. Manufacturing engineers can analyse machine and sensor data to improve operational efficiency and avoid downtime. Smart manufacturing facilitates the collection and analysis of data to reduce waste and improve productivity. It facilitates the circular economy and ensures sustainability for society.

PolySmart encompasses a broad spectrum of applications in biotechnology, environmental science, agri-food industries, and health processes, among others.

PHOTOSENS Erasmus Mundus Design Measures aims to establish a high-level, two-year joint Master’s program focused on the fabrication and application of photonic sensors for health and environmental monitoring. It will attract international students with strong academic backgrounds in mathematics, physics, engineering and electronics.

To address these challenges, we will form a consortium of five universities, sharing expertise to train future engineers and researchers in photonic sensing. Graduates will be equipped to design and fabricate components and systems that support health diagnostics, environmental monitoring and sustainability.

<< Background >>

One of the main causes of the present degradation suffered by our ecosystems is human action. This action is the result of the belief about the availability of inexhaustible sources of energy, due to which the human being has acted irresponsibly in the use and management of natural resources. The present paradigm of change and depletion of natural resources and other environmental problems require a global awareness of all actors in society, so that change occurs not only at the legislative and institutional level, but also at the individual level in favor of the collective good. . This is the main need addressed by the Revoluciónate en verde project. Although concrete actions are being carried out to preserve and care for our planet at the institutional level in Europe, there is still a long way to go at the individual level. We consider that one of the most important groups, given the impact of their activity on the environment, is the business fabric. For this reason, we have considered it essential to adequately train new European entrepreneurs in matters of sustainability and the environment for the sake of a more respectful and sustainable economic system.

<< Background >>

In 2021, a consortium of six partners from three European countries envisioned a project called Innovation for Open Ecosystems (I4OE), as a means to answer the questions: how can we support community stakeholders in adult education to engage and collaborate effectively in an open ecosystem? The main aim was to reach out to educators, local policy-makers, business decision-makers, non-governmental organizations, and members of civil society, adult learners and citizens overall, in order to empower them to promote cooperation, participation, and democratic citizenship in an educational context.
We argue that small-scale partnerships of the type investigated may guide quality development within education, with relevance to adult education quality and access initiatives. 
Therefore, I4OE was designed to help the community and relevant stakeholders to develop a framework that could be useful to identify local problems, so that they can work together to solve concrete challenges using a participatory approach, promoting democratic ideals. This is something that is not experienced as much in the adult education context, which we consider to be a need.

The project aim was to address the digital skills shortage within the cultural sector and improve digital access. It was done by creating a Competence center that holds and further develops knowledge database of guidance and tutor resources for open and free access. The project also develops methodologies and guidelines for introduction of the digital values chain standards into the performers’ skillsets. A demand arose in these cities: for someone to take on the task, with sensitivity and expertise, of processing grief, the loneliness in the face of the death of family members, but also the stories of those who, in healthcare facilities, communities, and nursing homes, accompanied these individuals until their last moments. The scarcity of resources and pandemic containment measures, in fact, have accentuated vulnerabilities and inequalities, disrupting individual lives, especially those of adults. << Background >>

Digital Partnerships for Creative Europe Association (DiPaCre) is strongly committed to bridging the technological divide and supporting the cultural and creative industries (CCI) in navigating the rapid digitalisation of their sector. From its founding, the association identified that independent stakeholders in the CCI are increasingly at risk of exclusion due to the complexity of new digital requirements. Issues such as managing digital metadata and complying with European Union directives—particularly the EU Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive (2019/790) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)—are creating significant barriers for these professionals to access the digital supply chain. Senior musicians, in particular, face considerable challenges in adapting to the digital environment. The project directly aligns with DiPaCre’s mission to empower the CCI community by offering free upskilling initiatives and educational resources, thus enabling independent artists to successfully engage with the digital marketplace and sustain their creative careers.

<< Background >>

After many years working in the field of employment guidance for people with disabilities, we have detected that the special employment centres, which is the model of protected employment in the case of Spain, carry out the largest number of hirings of people with disabilities compared to ordinary companies. For us, true inclusion is that which is carried out under equal conditions to the rest of the workers. From this arose the need to know the other models of sheltered employment in Europe, to make a comparative table in which to analyse the similarities and differences, as well as to take testimony from people with disabilities who currently develop their professional activity in sheltered employment. Always seeking to improve the working conditions of the group, we consider it important to initiate the process of creating a new model of sheltered employment under a quality framework that allows them access to employment, where their needs are respected without diminishing their labour rights (salary, leave, adaptations, etc.). Therefore, with this project we address the inclusion of people with disabilities in decent working conditions.

projects.title_en: Humor para la resiliencia: el clown como herramienta de intervención socio-terapéutica
projects.key_action: Partnerships for cooperation and exchanges of practices
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

We arrived at this proposal after identifying a twofold gap. On one hand, in our region an increasing number of migrants presenting anxiety, self-harm, or suicidal thoughts live in precarious conditions yet fail to meet the eligibility criteria for public mental health services—long waiting lists, language barriers, and a strictly clinical approach. On the other hand, both Casa Kuna and Ten Rock lacked an integrated methodology combining circus arts with psychosocial support: in Spain social circus remains at an early stage, while in Italy there were no specific tools tailored to vulnerable adult migrants.

We applied for this project to address these two shortcomings. We aimed to develop a practical guide that would transform clowning and other circus disciplines into a safe space for emotional regulation—easy to replicate in self-contained sessions—while simultaneously training our staff in brief evaluation techniques, intercultural facilitation, and a gender-sensitive perspective. Moreover, we needed a European framework to compare our findings, ensure the approach was transferable, and forge partnerships that would sustain this innovation beyond our local time

projects.title_en: 2024Women
projects.key_action: Partnerships for cooperation and exchanges of practices
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

In March 1976, the first International Tribunal on Crimes Against Women was held in Brussels, bringing together 2,000 women from 40 countries to testify about gender-based violence and discrimination. Led by feminists, the tribunal broke societal silence, influenced international legislation, and inspired local initiatives.

The women’s project in 2024 has provided an opportunity to launch a three-year participatory project to mark the 50th anniversary of the Tribunal in March 2026 in Brussels. This initiative addresses the need to: Reflect on the progress of women’s rights over the past 50 years; Highlight ongoing global gender inequalities and necessary reforms; Engage a new generation of women in raising awareness, sharing testimonies, artistic expression and advocacy.

Women24 participants are empowered, connected and supported to overcome the issues they face, with support from a growing network of experienced organisations. A wider platform of public professionals, academics and politicians are exploring how artistic and personal narratives can address modern gender injustices, creating a powerful space for solidarity, activism, and change.

We aimed to launch the LABECO project – a cooperative laboratory focusing on creative and ecological practices for all – in order to address several needs identified within our organisations and among our audiences:

>To strengthen the ecological skills of art and culture professionals, who are often aware of sustainable and inclusive practices but have little training in them.

>To experiment with informal learning formats adapted to adults in the arts and culture sector, in order to promote the transmission and dissemination of eco-responsible knowledge among priority audiences.

<< Background >>

VALUEU was proposed to develop and validate a scalable model linking Higher Education Institutions and Social Innovation Actors to strengthen Europe’s social innovation ecosystem. The pilot applies the EUt+ Citizen Lab and Ashoka’s Hybrid Value Chain within an Action Design Research framework to produce a hands‑on proof of concept that integrates social value into university innovation infrastructures and advances the European Universities initiative’s goal of open, cross‑border collaboration.

The project addressed persistent barriers: absent structures for sustained HEI–social innovation collaboration, unclear legal recognition of social innovation, and divergent academic and social value systems. Project was developed in response to a clearly identified need for a coherent and practical tool supporting the preparation of individuals in prison for their release. The analysis conducted by the Tulipan Foundation, based on extensive post-penitentiary experience and consultations with probation officers and representatives of the Prison Service, demonstrated the absence of a unified, operational pre-release programme that could be applied by educators, prison staff and NGOs. projects.title_en: Climate education topic days for primary classes that encourage children to be entrepreneurship
projects.key_action: Partnerships for cooperation and exchanges of practices
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

The CLIMENTRE project was developed in response to the urgent need to integrate climate literacy and environmental responsibility into early education and ennterprenoirship. Recognizing that behavioral patterns form between ages 3–10, we designed an educational model that introduces climate concepts and entrepreneurial thinking through twelve thematic learning days. These integrate sustainability across subjects and foster resilience, agency, and digital skills. Teachers often lack resources and confidence to address climate topics with young learners. CLIMENTRE fills this gap through research-based, multilingual, cross-curricular materials, piloted and refined in schools across partner countries. The project also addresses emotional well-being and aligns with EU climate goals, the UN SDGs, and Europe 2020. Through digital platforms and inclusive teaching tools, students are empowered to engage with global challenges while developing essential 21st-century skills. By supporting both educators and learners, CLIMENTRE offers a scalable, practical response to climate change through education—transforming schools into hubs of innovation, sustainability, and hope.

projects.title_en: You are incomplete without us to rescue the Earth
projects.key_action: Partnerships for cooperation and exchanges of practices
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

During the preparation phase of our project, we exchanged ideas with teachers in meetings. Some of the problems we observed in our school were that our students did not pay attention to water consumption, could not separate waste, and did not use electricity carefully. These problems were more pronounced among our students with special education needs.
According to the needs analysis we conducted with our partner schools, 64% of our students had very little knowledge about how plastic materials decompose in nature, the damage fossil fuels cause to the environment, the consequences of water and food waste, and the concept of recycling.
71% of the students polluted the environment unconsciously, and their carbon emissions were very high. In response to questions asked to teachers, it was revealed that 58% of them had no knowledge about carbon footprint. As a result of these analyses, we felt the need to educate our students about environmental pollution and climate change.
With our project, we aimed to improve teachers’ competencies in environmental pollution and climate change and to enable them to learn methods that would help students gain green skills

<< Background >>

We applied for the Erasmus Plus project with AquaSymphony to address urgent educational and environmental needs related to climate change and sustainable water use. As water scarcity becomes an increasingly critical global issue, we recognized a gap in teacher training and educational resources regarding this topic.

Our motivation stemmed from the understanding that teachers play a key role in shaping future generations' attitudes and behaviors. 
Thus, our project directly addresses these needs by:

Raising teacher awareness on climate change adaptation and sustainable water practices;

Improving their competencies and digital skills through targeted training and interdisciplinary learning modules;

Supporting language development and international collaboration;
And ultimately, producing a digitally supported teacher e-handbook to be used both locally and internationally, that will impact not only on teachers but also on hundreds of students and their families.
We strongly believe that empowering educators through this transnational initiative will generate a ripple effect, leading to greater environmental awareness and action at the community level and beyond.

projects.objective:
<< Background >>

Currently, there are around 3 000 clusters in the EU. Their members employ more than 50 million people, which represents approximately one in four jobs in Europe. Clusters serve as a link between science, business and administration. It is in them that industry, innovation, the labor market and education are concentrated. Their development is therefore extremely important for the European economy and depends largely on the competence of cluster coordinators, who are mostly responsible for management issues and the implementation of key projects. However, clusters lack people equipped with competences needed to deal with digital transformation issues.
Internal analyses done by the partners (interviews, workshops, cooperation with coordinators) identified the extent of the deficit in the aforementioned area, which are competences in:
•	Big Data/Data Science

<< Background >>

Youth unemployment rises more sharply and recovers more slowly than the average population. This is even more so for youngsters belonging to minorities and/or groups with fewer opportunities. Given that youngsters who are unable to enter the labour market are much more likely to result being long-term unemployed, lose their faith in their skills and even society as a whole, youth unemployment is a pressing issue that exceeds this particular generation. Anxiety,  antisocial behaviors and decreased optimism about the future of EU are only some of the effects of youth unemployment; the depth of this matter indicates the need for a collaborative, institutional approach
Youth organisations hold a key role in representing European youth. However, their capacities to be involved in institutional processes of decision making remains limited due to limited capacities in the field of policy and advocacy. Broadening and deepening the channels for youth involvement, particularly of youth with fewer opportunities, in the work and projects of civil society organisations is a prerequisite for achieving significant results - both for organisations and for participants themselves.

projects.title_en: EGSID - Empowering Grassroots Sport for Inclusion and Development
projects.objective:
The "Empowering Grassroots Sport for Inclusion and Development" (EGSID) project, set in Albania, is an initiative aimed at leveraging sports as a catalyst for societal benefits, particularly in promoting social inclusion, health, and well-being. The project specifically targets marginalized communities with the objective of enhancing their access to sports activities, thereby fostering a sense of belonging and community cohesion.
A key focus is on strengthening the organizational capacities of local sports entities to ensure they are more inclusive, effective, and sustainable. This includes providing training and resources to improve governance, management, and the delivery of sports programs that cater to diverse community needs.
Additionally, EGSID is committed to promoting European values, such as equality, non-discrimination, and human rights, within the sports sector. This aligns with broader efforts to encourage social change and tolerance through sports, highlighting the role of sports in bridging cultural and social divides.

projects.objective: Migration across borders in the European Union (EU) is a requirement in many elite sports and a crucial challenge for student-athletes (pursuing a Dual Career; DC). Policies vary across Europe and the existing support structures are not capable to overcome exchange obstacles. The insufficient support for migrating student-athletes is a major risk of decreased performances or drop-outs in education and sports. The AMiD project, therefore, aimed to assess and improve the current DC situation and migration opportunities in the EU. Academic partner institutions from five different European countries, each associated with one to two non-academic partners from the sports or DC sectors at national or European levels, plus the European Students as Athletes network represented the AMiD project team to conduct this project from 01/2018 until 12/2020.The first step was the assessment of the current situation. Pre-Covid, the European (including the UK) sports labour market had seen a 19.2% growth since 2011 (ESSA-Sport, 2020) but had structural workforce challenges, including an ageing managerial force, and it must now establish talent development, retention and employability strategies.

<< Objectives >>

The project aims to influence employability practices within the sport management discipline and to establish the need for individualistic labour market information (LMI) to complement traditional workforce planning data by analysing the career attitudes of students and sports managers.

Many elite and sub-elite sportspersons have part-time or full-time employment which is often characterised by a significant challenge to balance the demands of work and sport (i.e. Dual Career (DC)).  The value of the sportsperson to society and corporate brand is significant. BRAVA-DC (BRAnd Value Alignment through Dual Career) focused on how the circumstances and needs of DC employee sportspersons could be effectively accommodated while considering the needs and expectations of the employer.

<< Objectives >>

1) to structure an evidence and eminence knowledge base on DC employee athletes, and 2) to define and enable (i.e. feasible to implement) new European guidelines which support DC in the workplace and which facilitate appropriate brand alignment strategies and Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) policies which value DC. Accordingly, the project will inform the further operationalisation of the EU Guidelines on DC of Athletes (European Commission, 2012) in the specific context of the workplace.

projects.title_en: An educational and training program for older adults at risk of developing dementia through table tennis
projects.objective:
<< Background >>

The age distribution of the population is expected to change dramatically in the coming decades, with older people accounting for an estimated 16% of the population, up from 10% in 2022 (UN, 2022). There were an estimated 46.8 million people worldwide living with dementia in 2015, and this number is expected to almost double every 20 years (ADI, 2015). Therefore, it is critical to create cognitive and physical training programs, like table tennis, for people with dementia for rehabilitation.

<< Objectives >>

The hAlt project aims to investigate the potential of table tennis as a non-pharmacological intervention, combining physical and cognitive aspects, for older adults facing cognitive challenges. Studies suggest that regular aerobic exercise can reduce the risk of developing dementia by 28%, increasing to 45% for dementia specifically. The project aimed to engage people with mild dementia, those at risk of mild cognitive impairment, and table tennis coaches.

projects.objective:
Nearly half of young people change their health-related behaviours directly by accessing social media content (Goodyear et al., 2018). Indeed, social media is treated as a place where positive and harmful lessons about fitness health and the body are learned (Rick, 2018;  Toll & Norman, 2021). An IQVIA report (2020) identified that around 90,000 new digital health apps are shared annually in application stores. In sum, Young people increasingly use digital apps or social media as a source of health, diet and sports knowledge. While some young people benefit from this, others are affected negatively. However, there is a huge gap in research and policy understanding of the relationship between young people, social media/digital apps, health diet and sports, and the impacts. Consequently, uncontrolled contents are easily in circulation on social media and digital apps.

projects.objective:
Run and Recycle is a project that comes at an intense time for Europe. The invasion of Ukraine has changed the economy and the lives of every one of us, the effects of Covid-19 are still being felt, and against this backdrop the environmental crisis threatens to become a disaster - one of the reasons is "Fast Fashion".

The aim of Run and Recycle is to provide athletes with knowledge in textile waste management and to encourage the recycling of clothing and trainers used during training and competitions.
During the project 4 international meetings will take place. Each partner will organise 4 national eco-friendly running event and workshop to raise awareness on the topic. 

During the project we will create a common training manual on the topic and create guidelines to stimulate textile recycling. We will build a network of sports clubs that uphold environmental values. This network will include 50 sports organizations.

BENCHES involves five different sports: Athletics (with focus on Mountain Running), Biathlon, Canoeing and Kayaking, Football and Sailing. BENCHES will focus the interactions between these sports activities and nature, involving different terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems i.e.  mountains and forests in summer (Athletics) and winter period (Biathlon), urban biodiversity (Football), oceans, seas, rivers and lakes (Sailing, Canoeing and Kayaking), to assess, measure and find solutions to the pressures made by sport on biodiversity and to increase the awareness on ecosystems services evaluation.

projects.title_en: SLOPE - Ski Leans On the Promotion of the Environment
projects.objective:
The main objective of SLOPE is to enhance the knowledge of skiing’s impacts, risks and opportunities on biodiversity and to promote biodiversity capacity and management practices among national and international ski organizations. The project supports the integration of biodiversity management into governance frameworks and sustainability strategies, ensuring that winter sports organizations adopt effective solutions to reduce their environmental footprint.
By engaging key ski federations—including the French Ski Federation (FSF), the Norwegian Ski Association (NSF), the Estonian Ski Association (ESA), and the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS)—SLOPE fosters a systematic approach to biodiversity management at both the organizational and event levels. The project focuses on three distinct skiing ecosystems—the Alpine high-altitude mountains in France, the boreal lowlands in Estonia, and the subarctic fjord-mountains in Norway—allowing for a comprehensive assessment of biodiversity risks and pressures.
